q: When a potential difference is set up between the two ends of a conductor, a ____ flows through it.
e: When a potential difference is set up between the two ends of a conductor, a current flows through it. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path. A conductor lets charge drift when a potential difference is applied across it.

q: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady ____ is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.
e: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady potential difference is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path.

q: Batteries and generators are called sources of ____.
e: Batteries and generators are called sources of electromotive force. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by spinning conductors in a field.

q: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into ____ form.
e: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into electrical form. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into ____ form. electrical.

q: For example, a battery converts ____ energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.
e: For example, a battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power. Electrical power is the energy transfer rate, P = VI, also I^2R or V^2/R. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion.

q: In an electric generator, ____ energy is converted into electrical energy.
e: In an electric generator, mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy. A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by spinning conductors in a field. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion.

q: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a ____ terminal as shown in Figure 10.1.
e: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a negative terminal as shown in Figure 10. 1. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Positive terminal and a ____ terminal as shown in Figure 10.

q: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the ____ terminal within the source.
e: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the positive terminal within the source. From the negative terminal to the ____ terminal within the source. positive. A nearby word in place of positive would name a different quantity.

q: Alternately, it can be said that the main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the ____ terminal within the source.
e: Alternately, it can be said that the main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source. From the positive terminal to the ____ terminal within the source. negative. A nearby word in place of negative would name a different quantity.

q: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the ____ circuit.
e: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the complete circuit. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals.

q: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a ____.
e: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a force. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a ____. force.

q: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an ____ resistance.
e: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an internal resistance. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop.

q: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and ____.
e: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and temperature. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises.

q: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the resistor is $V=$____.
e: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the resistor is V=IR. Ohm's law is V = IR for ohmic parts at constant temperature. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat.

q: Similarly, the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance $r$ of the battery is ____.
e: Similarly, the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance r of the battery is Ir. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR+Ir$, which is the ____ $E$ of the battery.
e: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is IR+Ir, which is the emf E of the battery. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates.

q: The equation $E=IR+Ir$ is called the ____ equation.
e: The equation E=IR+Ir is called the circuit equation. The relation in this line is E=IR+Ir is called the ____ equation. A nearby word in place of circuit would name a different quantity.

q: Hence, the potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by $V=$____.
e: Hence, the potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by V=E-Ir. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals.

q: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always ____ than its emf.
e: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always less than its emf. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the ____ voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.
e: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the terminal voltage (or available voltage) of the battery. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises.

q: Hence, electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in an ____ circuit (when no current flows) as shown in Figure 10.3 (a).
e: Hence, electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in an open circuit (when no current flows) as shown in Figure 10.3 (a). Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. Current is charge passing a point each second, and it needs a closed path.

q: Terminal voltage(available voltage) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a ____ circuit as shown in Figure 10.3 (b).
e: Terminal voltage(available voltage) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit as shown in Figure 10.3 (b). Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals.

q: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a ____-circuit voltage.
e: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a closed-circuit voltage. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises.

q: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by ____ energy from some external source (battery charger) shown in Figure 10.4.
e: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by electrical energy from some external source (battery charger) shown in Figure 10.4. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (i) discharging (in use) $V=E-Ir$, $V$____$E$.
e: The terminal voltage of a battery when (i) discharging (in use) V=E-Ir, V<E. While discharging, voltage decays toward zero as a pure exponential with the same RC. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (ii) open circuit(not in use) $V=$____.
e: The terminal voltage of a battery when (ii) open circuit(not in use) V=E. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (iii) charging $V=E+Ir$, $V$____$E$.
e: The terminal voltage of a battery when (iii) charging V=E+Ir, V>E. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises.
